questions.title: Does Louisiana law require a physical signature on a premium finance company's cancellation certification?
questions.question_body: I'm reading *Williams v. GoAuto Insurance* and I'm confused about the court's interpretation of La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a). The statute requires the finance company to send a 'statement certifying' certain facts, but it doesn't explicitly mention a signature. The Plaintiffs argued that 'certifying' implies a signature, but the Fifth Circuit said no. Given Louisiana's 'strict adherence' doctrine for insurance cancellations, why is a signature not considered an implicit requirement of 'certification'? Does the text of the statute override the general expectation of a signature in legal certifications?

questions.title: Can an automated server's receipt of an email satisfy the statutory requirement of 'receipt' and 'possession'?
questions.question_body: In *Williams*, the court held that GoAuto's computer system receiving an email constituted 'receipt' under the statute, even though a human didn't physically take possession until later. The court cited Black's Law Dictionary definitions of 'receipt' and 'receive.' I'm struggling with the concept of a computer system 'taking possession.' If the statute requires the insurer to 'consider that cancellation... has been requested' upon receipt, does an automated trigger satisfy the intent of the legislature to ensure human oversight before a policy is terminated?

questions.title: What is the Fifth Circuit's standard for certifying questions of state law to the state supreme court?
questions.question_body: The Plaintiffs in *Williams* requested certification of the statutory interpretation issues to the Louisiana Supreme Court, but the Fifth Circuit denied it. The opinion cites *Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass'n* regarding the need for a 'compelling reason.' Can someone explain the specific threshold for certification in the Fifth Circuit? Why is the fact that a term has not been defined by the state supreme court insufficient to warrant certification, especially when it involves a significant insurance industry practice?

questions.title: How did the court distinguish *Benitez v. Elsayed* regarding the lack of employee identification on the notice?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses *Benitez v. Elsayed*, where a court noted a notice was not signed and did not identify a specific employee. However, the Fifth Circuit distinguished *Benitez* because the notices in *Williams* 'certified' the relevant information even without a named employee. I'm confused about the legal distinction here. If *Benitez* found the lack of identification problematic, why did the Fifth Circuit decide that the absence of a named employee didn't invalidate the certification in *Williams*? Does the word 'certify' carry more weight than the lack of a name?

questions.title: Does statutory compliance with cancellation procedures automatically preclude a breach of good faith claim?
questions.question_body: The Plaintiffs alleged both statutory violations and a breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. The district court dismissed *all* claims with prejudice after finding no statutory violation. The Fifth Circuit affirmed this. I don't understand the link between the two. If the statutory procedure was followed, does that automatically mean there was no bad faith? Can a company follow the letter of the statute but still act in bad faith, or does statutory compliance act as a complete defense to the tort claim in Louisiana insurance law?

questions.title: Why did the Fifth Circuit decline to address the District Court's 'private carrier' reasoning?
questions.question_body: The district court held that the APAC employee delivering the notices fit the definition of a 'private carrier' under the statute, which would have satisfied the delivery requirement. The Fifth Circuit found the e-mail sufficient and explicitly stated they would not consider the validity of the 'private carrier' definition. From a procedural standpoint, why did the appellate court avoid ruling on the district court's alternative legal theory? Does this mean the 'private carrier' definition remains unsettled law in the Fifth Circuit for Louisiana insurance cases?
